title: Demonstrate an understanding of the basic requirements of different fruit markets

lessons.title: Local and export fruit markets
lessons.html:
Where our fruit goes

South Africa is one of the biggest exporters of fresh fruit in the southern hemisphere. Citrus, apples, pears, table grapes, stone fruit and avocados go to many countries. Fruit that is not exported is sold locally or processed.

The main market types

MarketExamples
ExportEuropean Union, United Kingdom, Middle East, Asia (for example China, Japan), Russia, North America, Africa
Local fresh marketFresh produce markets such as Johannesburg and Cape Town, supermarket chains, informal traders
ProcessingJuice, canning, drying

Why markets are different

Each market has its own rules and customers. Buyers in one country may want small, very sweet mandarins, while another wants large oranges. Some want fruit in punnets or bags, others in loose cartons. Some markets pay a premium for top-quality fruit; others accept lower classes at lower prices.

What a market can specify

  • Quality class or grade: for example Class 1, or the export standards for that market.
  • Size or count range.
  • Colour and maturity standards.
  • Packaging: carton type, liners, punnets, bags, labels and language on labels.
  • Pallet type, height and labelling.
  • Chemical residue limits (MRLs): the maximum amount of a spray chemical allowed on the fruit, which differs between countries.
  • Phytosanitary (plant health) rules: to stop pests such as fruit fly or false codling moth entering the country.
  • Certification of farms and packhouses, such as GLOBALG.A.P. and customer-specific standards.

This is why the packhouse gives you a pack instruction for each order. The same fruit may be packed differently on the same day for different markets.

lessons.title: Meeting market requirements
lessons.html:
Who checks the fruit?

Export fruit from South Africa must be inspected before it leaves. The Perishable Products Export Control Board (PPECB) inspects fruit on behalf of the Department of Agriculture against the export standards and checks cold chain conditions. Some markets also need a phytosanitary certificate, and some require special protocols, such as cold treatment at set temperatures for set periods during shipping, to kill pests.

The buyer or importer may also inspect the fruit on arrival. If the fruit does not meet the specification, it can be rejected or the price cut.

Traceability

Markets require traceability: each carton must be traceable to the farm, orchard, packhouse and pack date. This is done through carton marks, pallet cards and records. If a problem is found, for example a chemical residue above the limit, the buyer can trace exactly where the fruit came from.

Residues and spray records

Farms must keep spray records and respect withholding periods so residues stay below each market's limit. Packhouses keep records of postharvest treatments. Because limits differ between countries, a batch may be allowed for one market but not another.

Food safety and social standards

Many buyers, especially supermarkets in Europe and the UK, want proof that fruit was produced safely and that workers were treated fairly. Packhouses and farms are audited for hygiene, worker health and safety, fair labour practice and environmental care.

What this means for you

  • Follow the pack instruction for each order exactly.
  • Never mix fruit from different producers, orchards or markets unless told to.
  • Use the correct labels and check that marks are correct.
  • Keep hygiene and cold chain rules.
  • Report anything that might break a market rule, such as insects found in fruit.

A single mistake can mean a whole container is rejected overseas, costing the farm hundreds of thousands of rand.

Key points

  • Fruit goes to export, local fresh and processing markets.
  • Each market has its own rules for grade, size, packaging and labels.
  • Markets set residue limits and plant health rules.
  • The PPECB inspects export fruit; buyers may inspect on arrival.
  • Traceability links each carton back to the farm and packhouse.
